title: Assay result corrected after sample-weight transcription check
initial_request: Please process the overnight HPLC assay sequence for lot DP26-041 and send the result to QA before the 10 a.m. batch meeting.
what_happened: The initial calculation gave 98.7% label claim, which was plausible and passed specification. During second-person verification, I found that the sample weight had been entered as 102.6 mg in the processing method, while the preparation worksheet showed 120.6 mg. I checked the balance printout and preparation log, corrected the entry, and reprocessed the sequence; the actual result was 84.0%, below specification. I invalidated the first draft report, documented the transcription error, and notified QA so an out-of-specification investigation could be opened.
error_consequence: The incorrect passing result could have supported release of an out-of-specification drug-product batch and triggered a data-integrity investigation once discovered.
why_or_why_not: An AI could flag disagreement between the worksheet and processing metadata, but I would not delegate the regulated data correction, audit-trail review, or final disposition because those require authorized human review and contemporaneous documentation.
persona: an analytical chemist running an LC-MS/HPLC lab in a mid-size pharma QC department

title: Impurity result reported as cannot report after bracket-standard failure
initial_request: Can you finish the related-substances sequence for API lot RM-11873? Manufacturing is waiting on the release result.
what_happened: The samples and first standard bracket processed normally, but the closing standard had only 82% of the opening-standard response, outside the method's 90-110% acceptance criterion. Reinjection from the same vial produced a similarly low response, and inspection showed a small air gap in the autosampler line after a solvent change. Because system suitability did not bracket the sample injections, I marked the run invalid and issued no impurity result rather than averaging the apparently acceptable sample values. The samples were freshly prepared and rerun after purging and priming the system.
error_consequence: Reporting from the failed sequence could have released raw material using unbracketed, potentially biased impurity measurements and created a compliance observation during audit.
why_or_why_not: I would delegate automatic detection and notification of the bracket-response failure, but not the decision to invalidate the run or the troubleshooting conclusion.
persona: an analytical chemist running an LC-MS/HPLC lab in a mid-size pharma QC department

title: LC-MS identity request delayed by ambiguous sample naming
initial_request: Please confirm the unknown peak in the stability sample by LC-MS; it should be the N-oxide. Samples are in the cold room under STAB-7.
what_happened: The cold-room rack contained three vials labeled STAB-7, STAB-7A, and STAB-7 repeat, while the request did not specify time point, strength, or preparation date. I compared the labels against the stability pull sheet and learned that STAB-7 was a study identifier rather than a unique sample identifier; one vial was also from an earlier exploratory preparation. After a short exchange with the requester, I documented the correct sample as the 40 mg, six-month accelerated time point and analyzed that vial alongside an N-oxide reference solution. The observed retention time and accurate mass supported the proposed identity, but I reported it as consistent with the N-oxide rather than definitively confirmed because no MS/MS reference spectrum was available.
error_consequence: Selecting the wrong vial could have attached an impurity identification to the wrong stability condition and distorted the product degradation assessment.
why_or_why_not: An AI could reconcile identifiers across the request, pull sheet, and chain-of-custody record and highlight ambiguities, but a chemist still needs to confirm sample identity and qualify the strength of the structural assignment.
persona: an analytical chemist running an LC-MS/HPLC lab in a mid-size pharma QC department

title: Recovered missing sequence provenance for an audit response
initial_request: QA needs the chromatograms, processing method version, and audit-trail explanation for sequence RS_260731_02 by end of day. The PDF in LIMS is missing two injections.
what_happened: The LIMS attachment was a manually assembled PDF that omitted two blank injections even though both were present in the CDS sequence. I exported a complete result set directly from Empower, verified the sample-set ID and processing-method checksum, and compared the injection timestamps with the instrument logbook. The audit trail showed that an analyst had changed peak integration for one low-level impurity and then restored the original method before approval; I included both events and the justification rather than supplying only the final chromatograms. QA accepted the replacement package and linked it to the original record without changing the reported results.
error_consequence: An incomplete or selectively packaged record could have led to an audit finding, delayed the regulatory response, and raised concerns about hidden injections or undocumented integration changes.
why_or_why_not: I would use AI to compare injection lists, identify missing pages, and draft an index of audit-trail events, but the provenance package and explanation require human verification against the validated CDS.
persona: an analytical chemist running an LC-MS/HPLC lab in a mid-size pharma QC department

title: Misassigned polyketide stereocenter caught by re-running ROESY at 600 vs 400 MHz
initial_request: Slack from postdoc: 'Can you look at compound 7 before I put it in the SI? I have the planar structure but I'm not 100% on the C-8/C-9 relative config. J(H8,H9) = 2.1 Hz so I called it syn.'
what_happened: I took the small J at face value and agreed with syn, and we drew it that way in a draft figure. Two weeks later I re-acquired ROESY on the 600 with a 300 ms mix (the original was a 400 MHz NOESY with 500 ms and had spin-diffusion smearing) and got a clear H-8/Me-19 correlation that is incompatible with syn. The 2.1 Hz was a rotamer-averaged value - the molecule was not conformationally locked, which I should have checked with a J-based configuration analysis of the 2,3JCH before trusting it. We ended up doing HetLOC/HSQC-HECADE and DP4+ on the two diastereomers to settle it as anti. Draft figure got corrected before submission but after it had been circulated to two collaborators.
files_and_tools: Gaussian 16 for DP4+ NMR shift calc
error_consequence: A wrong relative configuration in a published natural product; downstream synthesis group would have targeted the wrong diastereomer, and the correction would be a formal erratum.
why_or_why_not: The failure mode here was trusting one number without asking whether the conformation justified it. An AI could have flagged 'small J does not prove syn in a flexible chain' as a checklist item, which would actually have helped, but the actual call needed me looking at raw ROESY cross-peak signs and phasing for spin diffusion artifacts.
persona: an academic natural-products chemist who does NMR structure elucidation weekly

title: Cannot assign structure of 0.4 mg fraction from a marine cyanobacterium - reported as unassignable
initial_request: Email from PI: 'F17-3 is the active one in the antibiofilm assay (IC50 ~8 uM). We only got 0.4 mg. Please get whatever you can - can we at least get a formula and a partial structure for the grant report due the 14th?'
what_happened: HRESIMS gave a clean [M+H]+ at m/z 611.3641 and a plausible formula, but the 1H at 600 was a mess of overlapping methylenes between 1.2-1.6 ppm and the sample degraded visibly over the 36 h HSQC/HMBC run - a new set of peaks appeared and the original ones shrank by ~30%. HMBC from the first 12 h had maybe 6 usable correlations. I ran a diluted 1D in a Shigemi tube in CD3OD instead of DMSO-d6 to see if degradation was solvent-mediated; it was slower but the S/N was then too low for HMBC in the time we had. I wrote back that we can report the molecular formula, the presence of an N-methyl amide, two olefins and a likely peptide-polyketide hybrid, but that no connectivity beyond two fragments can be supported, and recommended re-isolating from a 20 L culture. PI wanted a proposed structure for the grant; I refused to put one in.
error_consequence: Publishing or even circulating a speculative structure from 6 HMBC correlations on a degrading sample - which the group has been burned by before - and then having to retract it after re-isolation.
why_or_why_not: The judgment call was 'is this enough evidence' under pressure from my own PI, which is a social/scientific call, not a data-processing one. That said I'd happily use an AI to help draft the diplomatic email explaining why we can't report it.
persona: an academic natural-products chemist who does NMR structure elucidation weekly

title: Reviewer asks for missing 13C data on three known compounds; hunting down 2019 raw data
initial_request: Reviewer 2, comment 4: 'The authors report compounds 3, 5 and 9 as known but do not provide 13C chemical shifts or comparison to literature values. Please provide a table of experimental vs. reported shifts, and deposit raw FIDs.'
what_happened: Two of the three compounds were run in 2019 by a student who has left; the FIDs were on a group NAS in folders named things like 'JL_new_frac_final_2' with no compound mapping. I cross-referenced acquisition timestamps against her scanned notebook PDFs to identify which dataset was which, and one turned out to be in acetone-d6 while the literature values were in CDCl3, so I had to re-run it. Built the comparison table in Excel with Delta-delta columns, found compound 5 deviated by 1.8 ppm at one carbon which turned out to be a referencing error in the original 2015 paper, not in our data, so I added a footnote. Then zipped the Bruker folders and uploaded to Zenodo with a README mapping compound numbers to folder names.
files_and_tools: MNova for reprocessing and referencing to residual solvent
error_consequence: Mismatched compound-to-FID mapping in a public deposition - embarrassing and hard to correct once DOI'd; also a wrong Delta-delta table would make a correct known-compound ID look wrong.
why_or_why_not: The lit-value lookup, table assembly and unit/referencing checks are exactly the tedious part I'd hand off, as long as I verify every literature citation myself - AI invents plausible chemical shifts and reference numbers. The FID-to-compound forensic matching needs the notebook context.
persona: an academic natural-products chemist who does NMR structure elucidation weekly

title: Phantom quaternary carbon that was a plasticizer/silicone contaminant
initial_request: Grad student, in person at the spectrometer: 'The HRMS says C20H24O5 which needs 20 carbons, but I only count 19 in the 13C. There's a carbon at 130.1 I can't get any HMBC to. Is it the missing one?'
what_happened: He wanted to place the 130.1 peak as an isolated quaternary olefinic carbon in the ring system, which would have forced a strained and frankly weird skeleton. I pulled up a blank CDCl3 spectrum from the same bottle and the 130.1 was there, along with 128.3 - it was styrene/plasticizer leached from the plastic pipette tip he'd used to transfer. The real missing carbon was a symmetry-degenerate pair (two equivalent aromatic carbons) that we confirmed by integrating the HSQC cross-peak intensity and by a long-relaxation-delay quantitative 13C run overnight (d1 = 30 s, inverse-gated). Rule now on the whiteboard: always run a solvent blank when a carbon has no HMBC correlations to anything.
files_and_tools: table of common NMR impurities (Fulmer et al. Organometallics 2010)
error_consequence: A published structure with a fictitious carbon and a strained skeleton - the kind of thing that gets a synthesis group's revision paper written about you.
why_or_why_not: Impurity-peak identification against a known table is exactly the pattern-matching an AI is good at, and 'check for common contaminants at 130.1/128.3/1.26/7.26' is a checklist I'd want run automatically on every spectrum. Final call still mine, but this would have saved the student two days.
persona: an academic natural-products chemist who does NMR structure elucidation weekly

title: Docking rerun after a protonation-state mismatch
initial_request: Can you dock the 18 new aminopyridines into the latest kinase structure and send poses before tomorrow's design meeting? Use the same setup as the last round.
what_happened: I copied the previous Glide workflow and obtained a plausible rank order, including a conserved hinge hydrogen bond for most compounds. During spot-checking, I noticed that the highest-ranked ligand had been imported as a neutral aminopyridine because the vendor SDF contained explicit hydrogens and formal charges inconsistent with our SMILES table. I regenerated protonation states from the registered SMILES at pH 7.4 plus or minus 1.0, reran the set, and found that six compounds changed preferred orientation and the original top-ranked compound dropped to ninth. I sent the corrected table and marked the first output as invalid rather than trying to reconcile the two scores.
error_consequence: The team could have prioritized synthesis of compounds based on an artifact of an incorrectly neutralized ligand, costing roughly a chemistry cycle and several assay slots.
why_or_why_not: An AI could compare identifiers or flag charge inconsistencies, but I would not delegate the final protonation choices or pose assessment because they depend on chemical context, binding-site interactions, and inspection of generated structures.
persona: a computational chemist supporting a medicinal chemistry team (docking, QSAR, conformers)

title: QSAR update blocked by inconsistent assay definitions
initial_request: Please add the latest cellular potency data to the permeability model and tell us whether the new morpholine series is predicted to be clean.
what_happened: The request mixed two endpoints: the existing model predicted MDCK apparent permeability, while the attached spreadsheet contained a cellular EC50 assay and an efflux-ratio column from a different protocol. I traced the workbook tabs and the assay registration records, then asked whether a new cellular-potency model was intended or whether the team wanted MDCK predictions for the new structures. The requester confirmed that the needed MDCK measurements had not yet been loaded and that the cellular data were attached by mistake. I returned a cannot-report result for model performance or series classification and provided a list of 27 compound IDs awaiting the correct endpoint.
error_consequence: Treating EC50 values as permeability labels would have produced a meaningless validation statistic and could have led the team to discard or advance the series for the wrong property.
why_or_why_not: I would delegate column-name comparison, unit detection, and drafting the missing-data list to an AI, but require a scientist to verify endpoint identity and approve the cannot-report conclusion.
persona: a computational chemist supporting a medicinal chemistry team (docking, QSAR, conformers)

title: Conformer generation failure caused by atropisomer handling
initial_request: Generate up to 200 conformers for these 63 macrocycle ideas so we can calculate shape similarity to the lead; default settings are fine.
what_happened: OMEGA completed most compounds, but nine produced fewer than five conformers and three returned no structures despite having valid-looking SMILES. Inspection showed that two inputs had undefined atropisomeric axes and one macrocycle contained a coordinate bond encoded in a way the toolkit interpreted as a standard single bond. I normalized the structures, separated the atropisomer cases into explicitly enumerated records, and reran with macrocycle sampling enabled while retaining the original stereochemistry labels. Seven compounds then produced usable ensembles, but I reported two as failed because their intended stereochemistry could not be established from the design file.
error_consequence: Silent stereochemical expansion or malformed conformers would have contaminated shape-similarity rankings and could have made inaccessible stereoisomers appear attractive.
why_or_why_not: An AI could triage log messages, identify records with low conformer counts, and prepare a retry manifest, but explicit stereochemical interpretation and acceptance of the ensembles need human review.
persona: a computational chemist supporting a medicinal chemistry team (docking, QSAR, conformers)

title: Packaging a docking comparison with receptor and ligand provenance
initial_request: Can you send the docking summary for the two backup scaffolds, preferably one slide with scores and pictures, for the project update at 3?
what_happened: The two scaffold sets arrived in separate spreadsheets using local compound names, and four names mapped to multiple registration IDs. I resolved the identifiers against the registry, selected representative poses only after checking strain, hinge geometry, buried unsatisfied polar atoms, and agreement with the redocked reference ligand. The score difference between the scaffolds was within the variation seen across two receptor preparations, so I labeled the comparison inconclusive rather than naming a docking winner. I delivered one slide plus a CSV manifest containing structure IDs, ligand states, receptor preparation hashes, grid version, and pose filenames.
error_consequence: An overconfident scaffold ranking or an image tied to the wrong compound ID could have biased the project team toward a synthesis plan unsupported by the calculation.
why_or_why_not: I would use AI to draft captions, check that IDs and filenames agree across the slide and manifest, and summarize caveats, but not to select poses or decide whether the score difference is meaningful.
persona: a computational chemist supporting a medicinal chemistry team (docking, QSAR, conformers)

title: Empower audit trail review flagged 'missing' injections that weren't missing
initial_request: Slack from QA lead: 'Can you pull the audit trail for project QC-2024-STAB for the last quarter? Auditor wants to see all deletions/modifications. Need it by Thursday.'
what_happened: I ran the Empower Audit Trail report filtered by project and date range and found 14 entries showing injections marked 'Deleted' by a specific analyst. I wrote it up as a potential integrity concern and sent a heads-up to QA before finishing. Two days later, while cross-checking sample set method IDs, I realized the deletions were of the *result sets*, not raw injection data, and the raw data was intact and still linked to a later reprocessing. The report column header was 'Object Deleted' and I'd conflated object types because the export flattened the type field. I had to send a correction, and QA had already opened a preliminary deviation, which then needed to be closed with a rationale. Now I always pull the ObjectType column explicitly and re-verify against the project tree before writing anything.
files_and_tools: Toolkit/Oracle query via DBA read-only account
error_consequence: Falsely accusing a named analyst of data deletion; an unnecessary deviation record that itself becomes an inspection finding about our own investigation quality.
why_or_why_not: The whole failure was semantic - knowing what an Empower 'result set' vs 'injection' vs 'channel' means in the audit trail schema, and that our export drops a type column. An AI could summarize the CSV fine but would make the exact same conflation, and this output goes to a regulator.
persona: a laboratory informatics manager responsible for data integrity and instrument software

title: Cannot confirm 21 CFR Part 11 compliance of a benchtop NMR because the vendor won't say who can edit the config file
initial_request: Email from the analytical development director: 'We're buying the [vendor] benchtop NMR, PO is drafted. Can you sign off that the software is Part 11 compliant? Should be quick, they say it is.'
what_happened: I sent the vendor our standard supplier assessment questionnaire and got back a marketing PDF saying 'Part 11 ready.' Pushed for specifics: the acquisition software stores its user roles in a plain XML file on the local machine, and the audit trail is a text log in the same directory. I installed the demo on a sandbox VM, logged in as a standard Windows user, and successfully edited both the roles XML and the log with Notepad, then relaunched and the software accepted it. I wrote the assessment as 'cannot recommend for GMP use in current configuration' rather than pass/fail, listing three specific gaps and the compensating controls (locked-down OS, no local admin, data copied to the network share on a schedule) that would be needed. Procurement was annoyed; the instrument was bought for R&D-only use with a hard restriction in the SOP.
error_consequence: Signing off would have put a non-compliant system in the GMP data path; every result on it becomes questionable at the next inspection, potentially invalidating stability data.
why_or_why_not: The evidence came from actually breaking the thing on a VM. No amount of document reading would have found it - the vendor's own docs claim compliance. AI could help draft the writeup wording afterward though.
persona: a laboratory informatics manager responsible for data integrity and instrument software

title: LIMS-to-instrument worklist import failing silently on sample IDs with a leading zero
initial_request: Ticket, priority Medium, from a micro analyst: 'worklist import doesn't work sometimes. samples are missing. it worked last week.' No screenshots.
what_happened: Took two rounds of back-and-forth to get an actual example - the analyst had already re-typed the missing rows manually so the original file was overwritten. Eventually got a fresh failing case and diffed it against a working one: the LIMS export writes sample IDs as text, but somebody in the middle of the chain was opening the CSV in Excel to 'check it' and saving, which stripped leading zeros from IDs like 0034521, and the instrument software then found no match and skipped the row without any error dialog. Fixed by changing the LIMS export to .txt with a tab delimiter and adding a row-count reconciliation step to the SOP. Also filed a bug with the instrument vendor about the silent skip - still open eight months later.
error_consequence: Silently missing samples in a micro ID run - results reported against the wrong sample or a sample quietly never tested, which is a batch release problem.
why_or_why_not: The diagnosis step - 'diff these two files and tell me every character-level difference in the ID column' - is exactly the boring thing I'd hand off. I'd still do the root-cause conversation with the analyst and the SOP change myself.
persona: a laboratory informatics manager responsible for data integrity and instrument software

title: Time-zone drift on three HPLC data systems found during a routine periodic review
initial_request: Recurring calendar item: 'Q3 periodic review - chromatography data systems. Check NTP sync, orphan users, backup restore test.'
what_happened: Ran the usual check comparing each acquisition PC's clock against the domain controller. Three PCs in the QC lab were 61 minutes off - they'd been imaged from a template that had the time zone set but 'automatically adjust for daylight saving' unchecked, so they drifted at the DST changeover in March and nobody noticed for five months. Timestamps in the audit trail for those instruments were therefore an hour behind reality for all runs in that window. I had to scope it: pulled the injection list for the affected period, confirmed no sequence-of-events determination depended on cross-instrument timestamp comparison, documented it as a minor deviation with an impact assessment, and pushed a GPO to enforce the DST setting. The restore test also failed on one archive volume, unrelated, which ate another day.
files_and_tools: Excel pivot for the injection list
error_consequence: If timestamp accuracy had mattered for an investigation in that window - e.g. proving a sample was run after a re-standardization - the data would have been unusable and the affected results potentially invalidated.
why_or_why_not: Detecting the drift is trivially automatable and honestly should already be a monitoring alert - that part yes. But the impact scoping required knowing which of our investigations actually rely on timestamp ordering, which is institutional knowledge and a judgment call I have to own on the deviation record.
persona: a laboratory informatics manager responsible for data integrity and instrument software
